newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe commodity exchange chips trade from state.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe commodity exchange chips trade from state.

text.p: Zimbabwe's private agricultural commodity exchange is slowly chipping away trade from the country's dominant state agency, which was slow to process payments, a senior trade official said on Friday.

Zimbabwe Agricultural Commodities Exchange (ZIMACE) administrator Ian Goggin said after some initial hesitancy many farmers have become familiar with the operations of his exchange, the first of its kind in Africa.

Before its establishment in March 1994, Zimbabwean farmers were forced to sell their crop to the government-owned Grain Marketing Board (GMB) and many were unhappy with the producer prices pre-set for them by the board.
On the ZIMACE market traders can buy and sell maize, wheat, soybeans, cotton seed and beans at spot and forward-quoted prices.
Goggin said an increasing number of farmers, disgruntled over delays by the GMB in paying them for their crop, were now opting to trade through the exchange.

"The ZIMACE contract guarantees payment within 14 days as compared with the six months or even longer it takes for GMB to pay farmers," he said, adding that traders were also attracted by the availability of arbitration in case of disputes.

He said since the beginning of the marketing season in April, over Z$210 million (U.S.$19.5 million) worth of trade had been done on the exchange, compared with Z$195 million for the whole of last season.
Zimbabwe's staple maize crop had accounted for 28,000 tonnes of trade worth about Z$34.5 million compared to the previous season's 19,055 tonnes which fetched Z$26.6 million.
Goggin said wheat volumes had also leaped to 45,000 tonnes from 5,500 tonnes last season, with trade in soybeans jumping to 40,000 tonnes from 7,500 tonnes.
He said there had been progress towards achieving increased regional trade in agricultural commodities, with several consultative meetings having been held in South Africa and Kenya this year.
But he added there was still need for dialogue between governments to formulate policies that would pave the way for regional trade.
"We're still hamstrung by government policies at the moment but the main thing is that we're now exchanging views and communicating much better than we used to," Goggin said.
